title: Hard to be called a Muslim
word: Hard to be called a Muslim
hookLine: it is hard to be called a true Muslim; first love the faith and let go of pride (Majh ki Var, ang 141)

lines: HARD TO BE CALLED A MUSLIM.
cards: A cast-iron pan comes out of the back of a cupboard, orange with rust. Steel wool, hot water, patience, and slowly the dark metal shows again. Nobody calls it clean until it is.
Guru Nanak lived among Hindus and Muslims, and in his ballad in Majh he speaks to his Muslim neighbors in the words of their own faith. He doesn't tell anyone to stop being a Muslim.
He says something harder, in plain English: it's difficult to be called a Muslim. Only if you truly are one should you be called one.

teach.h: FIRST, LET THE FAITH BE SWEET.
teach.b: The salok goes on, not word for word. First, let the faith be sweet to you.
Scrape away pride in your wealth, the way rust is scraped from metal. Become a true follower of the faith, and be rid of doubt about death and life. Accept God's will as above your head.
Trust the Creator, and lose your self-importance. Be kind to every living being, says Nanak, and then you may be called a Muslim. Notice how high the bar is, and whose bar it is.
Its words, din, faith; raza, God's will; mihar, mercy, are words his Muslim neighbors used for their own faith.

He isn't laying a new standard over them; he's taking their own words seriously and asking that they be lived all the way through. A few lines before, on ang one hundred forty, he does the same with the outward signs.
In paraphrase: let mercy be your mosque, faith your prayer mat, and honest living your Quran. Modesty, good conduct, truth: each a practice of the faith, lived inside. And the salok mocks no one.
Elsewhere on this path Nanak asks the same of pandits and yogis: live what your name promises.
Muslims here are honored by being held to their own best words. Notice the order, too. First, sweetness, before rules or outward signs.
The salok calls this hard. It doesn't call it impossible.
That's today's line: hard to be true.

how: These saloks are sung and read as part of Majh ki Var in the Guru Granth Sahib, and in katha they are explained as Guru Nanak asking people of every faith to live what their own faith teaches.

games.q: what does “hard to be called a muslim” mean?
o: a saying that faith is too hard for most people
a name earned by living the faith's own best words
a rule that only scholars may call themselves Muslim

games.q: what's inside the salok — tap the pairs.

s: Guru Nanak tells Muslims to stop being Muslims
he asks them to be Muslims truly, in their own faith's words: sweetness, surrender, mercy.
the salok says kindness to every living being is part of the name
be kind to every being, says Nanak, and then be called a Muslim.
the salok calls living up to the name impossible
it calls it hard, and then lays out the steps.

games.q: you carry the name of your faith. in Guru Nanak's salok, what comes first?
o: letting the faith be sweet to you.
games.why: first, let the faith be sweet; then scrape away pride, accept God's will, and be kind to every being.

practice: Name quietly what you're called: the faith you belong to, the one you're learning, or a simpler name like friend, parent, neighbor.
Ask gently what that name promises, find one word in it, kindness, honesty, patience, mercy, and hold it for a few breaths. If you pray, offer that word to God in the way your own tradition prays.

wordCard.voice: Hard to be called a Muslim. Guru Nanak's salok in Majh ki Var: let the faith be sweet, scrape away pride, accept God's will, be kind to every being, and then be called by the name. Today's word.

orig.note: musalman kahavan muskal: 'it is hard to be called a Muslim', the salok's opening.

carryVoice: Your line: hard to be true. Hard, and still worth the scouring, like that old pan. Until tomorrow.
